shared.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
shared.bigQuestion: When does technology strengthen our learning—and what choices keep the thinking, safety, and responsibility with us?
shared.summary: During the Grade 6 rotations, students work through fast, concrete technology and AI decisions. In pairs and table groups they test whether authorship can be guessed from style, sort six classroom situations, repair a shortcut prompt, challenge a confident AI response, and propose a usable class commitment. Each student then writes and signs a one-page learning, technology, and AI agreement for the teacher who will receive them.

learningArc.label: Launch
learningArc.studentAction: Name one learning job a tool can help with and one choice that could weaken trust.
learningArc.outcome: Technology is discussed through learning purposes and responsible decisions, not app popularity.

learningArc.label: Detect
learningArc.studentAction: Vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL for three samples, then point to evidence and its limits.
learningArc.outcome: Students replace style-based guesses with questions about process, sources, drafts, and explanation.

learningArc.label: Sort
learningArc.studentAction: Place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK and defend the call.
learningArc.outcome: Students reason with privacy, accuracy, ownership, attribution, and learning purpose.

learningArc.label: Prompt
learningArc.studentAction: Repair a prompt so AI questions and coaches instead of completing the work.
learningArc.outcome: The learner's decisions, evidence, and final explanation remain visible.

learningArc.label: Repair
learningArc.studentAction: Mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one weak claim.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate useful language from reliable evidence.

learningArc.label: Draft
learningArc.studentAction: Write and stress-test one table commitment using a real scenario.
learningArc.outcome: The class gathers observable commitments rather than broad slogans.

learningArc.label: Agree
learningArc.studentAction: Complete a personal learning, technology, and AI agreement.
learningArc.outcome: Each student names a support, a commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, and a teacher question.

learningArc.label: Sign
learningArc.studentAction: Check, sign, and place the named page in the rotation collection tray.
learningArc.outcome: The receiving teacher gets a practical starting point for a follow-up conversation.

visual.alt: Grade 6 students working in table groups with paper decision cards while one teacher-controlled screen supports the discussion.
visual.caption: One shared decision lab: talk first, make a call, test the reasoning, and revise.

primaryResource.label: Download the student agreement
primaryResource.description: My Grade 6 Learning, Technology & AI Agreement—the individual handoff completed during minutes 50–60.

thinkingMoves.label: Ask better questions
thinkingMoves.prompt: What question would reveal the process or evidence?

thinkingMoves.label: Verify
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which claim matters enough to trace to a current, named source?

thinkingMoves.label: Challenge assumptions
thinkingMoves.prompt: What are we assuming from style, confidence, or convenience?

thinkingMoves.label: Weigh trade-offs
thinkingMoves.prompt: What does this choice strengthen, and what responsibility does it create?

thinkingMoves.label: Improve
thinkingMoves.prompt: How can we revise the prompt, response, or commitment so it works in a real situation?

thinkingMoves.label: Reflect
thinkingMoves.prompt: What choice will help me learn and make my process honest and visible?

teacher.grouping: Pairs for the opening exchange; tables of 3–4 for evidence calls, prompt repair, response audit, and one shared commitment; individual work only when personalization is the purpose—the student's own agreement; whole-class reveals between rounds.
teacher.launch: A Grade 6 class can use conversation, paper, a projector, devices, search, and AI. Which jobs should tools help with—and which choices keep the learning trustworthy?
prepare: Download and print one My Grade 6 Learning, Technology & AI Agreement per student; add one labelled collection tray for each rotation group.
Open First Week Mission in Teach / Project mode and check that the Detect, Sort, Prompt, and Repair controls advance correctly.
Prepare three large table-lane cards: HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, and STOP + ASK; paper or hand signals also work.
Place one large paper and marker at each table for the class-commitment draft.
If using a teacher-approved AI session for the prompt test, open it before students arrive. The prepared on-screen response completes the same reasoning route.
Confirm exact bell time and who receives the clipped, named agreement sets after classes are formed.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Give 20 silent seconds, a 45-second partner exchange, then collect two helpful uses and two possible problems.
Run all three HUMAN / AI / CANNOT TELL samples. Require a clue and its limit before revealing.
Run at least four exact scenarios, including private details and a confident local fact with no source.
Compare the three prompts. Have tables identify the wording that keeps the claim, evidence, and final decision with students.
Assign each numbered AI sentence to a table. Record what to keep, what evidence is needed, and what students must rewrite.
Each table writes ‘When ___, we will ___ because ___.’ Stress-test every proposal against a scenario and combine overlaps.
Students complete their own agreement. Confer on commitments that are too broad; support writing with dictation or labelled drawings.
Students remove private account details, sign, and submit. Check names, clip by rotation, and explain the receiving teacher follow-up.

scenarios.title: Question brainstorm
scenarios.situation: After listing three ideas, a pair asks AI for five more inquiry questions, chooses one, and rewrites it.
scenarios.reason: The pair begins, compares, chooses, and explains.

scenarios.title: Confident local fact
scenarios.situation: AI gives a precise Fleetwood population number with no source or date for a class poster.
scenarios.reason: Trace an important number to a current, named source.

scenarios.title: Private details
scenarios.situation: A chatbot requests a full name, school schedule, account name, and photo to personalize a study plan.
scenarios.reason: Do not enter identifying or account information; ask for an approved route.

scenarios.title: Finished reflection
scenarios.situation: A student pastes an AI-written final reflection and cannot explain one of its claims.
scenarios.reason: The tool replaced the learner's evidence and reflection.

scenarios.title: Another fair test
scenarios.situation: A table asks AI for another variable to control, judges the suggestion, runs the test, and records its own results.
scenarios.reason: AI offers a possibility; students decide and gather the evidence.

scenarios.title: Invented voice
scenarios.situation: AI offers to speak as a named Indigenous Elder instead of using an attributed Nation or First Nations-led source.
scenarios.reason: A simulation cannot replace a living person's or Nation's voice.

lookFors: Names the learning purpose a tool serves instead of treating the tool as the goal.
Says CANNOT TELL when style alone cannot establish whether a human or AI made something.
Defends a scenario call with privacy, accuracy, ownership, attribution, or learning—not a vague feeling.
Repairs a prompt so the learner still chooses the claim, evidence, and final wording.
Checks confident claims and distinguishes polished language from reliable evidence.
Contributes to table reasoning and can explain the group's commitment independently.
Writes one observable personal commitment, one stop-and-ask moment, one useful support, and one teacher question.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Treat the table decision trail and commitment as formative observation only. Clip each student's named agreement by rotation date, sort once by final roster, and pass it privately to the receiving teacher for acknowledgement and follow-up. Do not grade the agreement, use it for class placement, post it to SpacesEDU, or treat the signature as consent to create accounts or use a tool.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
student.why: You will use technology, search, and sometimes AI during Grade 6. This lab helps you know what to check, what to keep as your own thinking, what information to protect, and when to ask for help.
student.summary: Work with a partner and table to investigate realistic classroom choices. You will make evidence-based calls, improve a prompt and an AI response, help write a class commitment, and finish with an agreement in your own words.
student.grouping: Partner talk and tables of 3–4 for the investigations; your personal agreement is individual because it describes your commitments, supports, and question.
bring: A pencil or another way to record your ideas
Your reasons, questions, and willingness to change your mind
No passwords, account names, photos, schedules, or private family information
student.firstMove: Think of one time technology helped you imagine, practise, organize, check, communicate, create, access support, or collaborate. Tell a partner what it helped you do.

quickReference.firstMove: Tell a partner about one time technology helped you learn. Name what it helped you do.
quickReference.handIn: Put your named agreement in the rotation tray. It is practice, not a grade.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the short scenario and agreement. Use the four-question check if you get stuck.

student.firstMoveNote: Name the learning job, not just the app or device. Then predict one choice that could make the result less useful or trustworthy.
steps: Detect: vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL and explain what your clue can prove.
Sort: place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK.
Prompt: turn ‘do it for us’ into a prompt that asks questions and waits for student decisions.
Repair: mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one problem.
Draft: help your table write one commitment that tells people what to do in a real moment.
Agree: choose two class commitments and write one commitment of your own.
Personalize: name one support that helps you learn, one stop-and-ask moment, and one teacher question.
Sign and submit: check that the agreement sounds like you and contains no private account information.
choices: Use speaking, writing, pointing, table cards, dictation to an adult, or labelled drawings to show your reasoning.
Disagree with a table call when you can give a reason tied to learning, privacy, accuracy, ownership, or fairness.
Describe a school-learning support that is useful to your teacher; private medical, diagnostic, or family details are not required.
student.product: One table commitment plus your signed, one-page My Grade 6 Learning, Technology & AI Agreement.
student.finish: You can explain one decision your thinking group made, show how a prompt or response was improved, and submit an agreement with a specific commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, a learning support, and a teacher question.
student.handInOrSave: Place the named agreement in the labelled rotation tray. It goes privately to your receiving Grade 6 teacher as the start of a conversation; it is not graded.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: If absent, ask for the short scenario-and-agreement route. If stuck, choose one situation and use four questions: What is the learning purpose? Is private information involved? What needs checking? Who makes the final decision?
student.spacesNote: The named agreement is not posted to SpacesEDU. Later in September, you may choose stronger evidence for a Learning Story about how your thinking changed.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: The first Grade 6 technology decisions
family.summary: During the opening rotations, students spend one 60-minute lesson investigating realistic choices about search, devices, and AI. The focus is practical: privacy, checking claims, keeping student thinking visible, explaining help received, and knowing when to stop and ask an adult.
family.whyThisMatters: Students need more than a slogan such as ‘use AI responsibly.’ They practise making and defending a decision in situations they may actually encounter, including a confident claim with no source, a request for private information, and a tool that offers to complete the student's work.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students first work in pairs and tables to examine three authorship samples, sort six scenarios, repair a shortcut prompt, audit four claims in an AI response, and write one testable table commitment. In the final ten minutes, each student completes and signs an individual learning, technology, and AI agreement.

quickReference.atSchool: In pairs and table groups, students sort six realistic situations, improve an AI prompt and response, then write their own one-page agreement.
quickReference.home: Nothing to prepare or finish at home.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher observes reasoning and revision. The agreement is practice—not a grade or placement decision.
quickReference.spaces: The agreement stays with the teacher. Selected learning and feedback may appear in SpacesEDU later.

family.product: A table contributes one proposed class commitment. Each student submits a one-page agreement naming a useful learning purpose, two class commitments, one personal commitment, a stop-and-ask situation, a learning support, and a question for the receiving teacher.
family.assessment: This is low-stakes formative evidence. The teacher listens for clear reasons, willingness to verify, respect for privacy and authentic voices, honest explanation of tool help, and the student's ability to keep final decisions visible. The agreement is not graded and does not affect class placement.
family.agreementNote: This is a student-to-teacher learning agreement, not a legal contract or family consent form. It does not give permission to create accounts or use unapproved tools, and it does not replace Surrey Schools policies or teacher directions. Commitments may be discussed and revised as the class learns.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Table talk shows how students compare evidence, share airtime, and revise a decision. The individual page preserves each student's own commitment, support, and question. Named completed agreements stay private with the teacher.

shared.title: Five ways to become known
shared.bigQuestion: What can we learn about ourselves, one another, and this place without asking anyone to share a private story?
shared.summary: Across five connected days, students tell a low-risk object story, show how they reason with number size, name useful learning conditions, gather exact observations from the school grounds, and choose one specific example for a Friday Learning Story.

learningArc.label: Story
learningArc.studentAction: Choose an ordinary object, point to five visible clues, tell a three-beat story, and improve it after one listener question.
learningArc.outcome: The class begins with voice, listening, visible evidence, and a safe fictional route.

learningArc.label: Number
learningArc.studentAction: Place very large and very small quantities on accurate scales and explain one surprising position.
learningArc.outcome: The teacher sees strategies and misconceptions without reducing students to a score.

learningArc.label: Learning
learningArc.studentAction: Test which conditions help in real classroom situations and write one useful request or strategy.
learningArc.outcome: Students describe changeable supports and actions rather than fixed learning labels.

learningArc.label: Place
learningArc.studentAction: Collect exact sound, movement, colour, light, and texture evidence outside or from an equivalent observation station.
learningArc.outcome: Observation stays separate from inference, and the class gathers material for a place response.

learningArc.label: Synthesize
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one specific example, name what it shows, set one realistic goal, and revise for a teacher or family audience.
learningArc.outcome: One meaningful Learning Story replaces several small uploads.

visual.alt: Grade 6 students sharing an object story, comparing number evidence, making notes, and observing the school grounds in pairs and small groups.
visual.caption: Five connected ways to notice how students think, contribute, communicate, and learn.

thinkingMoves.label: Notice exactly

thinkingMoves.label: Listen for meaning
thinkingMoves.prompt: What did your partner actually say, show, or choose?

thinkingMoves.label: Explain a strategy
thinkingMoves.prompt: What did you try, and why did it make sense?

thinkingMoves.label: Revise from feedback
thinkingMoves.prompt: What one change makes the idea clearer or more accurate?

thinkingMoves.label: Choose useful evidence
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which specific example says something important about your learning?

teacher.launch: This week gives us five different ways to notice how people think and learn. Nobody has to share a private or painful story. We will use specific evidence, listen carefully, and revise one idea each day.
prepare: Open the First Formed Class Week preset in Week Plan and add exact bells, support, supervision, and school events.
Prepare the ordinary-object image sets or six safe objects, number cards or scrap paper, and a safe soundwalk plus seated/window alternative.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Model one low-stakes three-beat story, then protect partner telling, listener questions, and one clear retell.
Use the projected number scale, require predictions before reveals, and record strategies rather than ranking students.
Use classroom cases, avoid fixed labels, and have students name one support or action they can explain.
Teach observation versus inference, follow the safe route, and offer an equivalent stationary or indoor route.
Students choose one strong example, add a realistic goal and first step, revise for an audience, and make the single September post.

lookFors: Points to exact story, number, or place evidence before making an inference.
Listens closely enough to ask a useful question or restate a partner's idea accurately.
Explains a strategy, support, contribution, or revision with a specific example.
Uses the Friday Learning Story to synthesize the week instead of uploading five separate activities.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Use conversation, notebooks, quick models, observation, and conferences as formative evidence. Friday's student-selected Learning Story is the only planned SpacesEDU post from this sequence; do not require private disclosure or turn the midweek learning profile into a second post.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Our first week together
student.why: Your teacher needs more than one kind of evidence to understand how you think, communicate, contribute, and learn.
student.summary: Tell, estimate, notice, discuss, move, create, and reflect across five connected days. You can use fictional examples and school-learning information; private details are never required.
student.grouping: Partners and table groups most days; one individual Friday Learning Story
student.routeTitle: Five ways to show your learning
bring: Pencil or another way to record
student.firstMove: Choose one ordinary object. Point to five details you can truly see before you invent a story.
student.firstMoveNote: Stay with what you can point to first. Your story may be fictional, but its visible clues should be honest.

quickReference.firstMove: Choose an object and point to five visible clues before you invent.
quickReference.handIn: Keep Monday–Thursday work in class. On Friday, post one Learning Story when your teacher asks.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the day's image, question, and one example. Recover the important thinking—not every missed minute.

steps: Tell: build a short object story from visible clues.
Estimate: place and explain very large and very small numbers.
Name: identify a learning condition or action that helps in a real situation.
Notice: collect exact evidence from the school grounds or an equivalent observation station.
Reflect: choose one specific example and set one realistic goal.
choices: Show thinking by speaking, writing, drawing, pointing, moving, building, or using a teacher-supported communication route.
Use a fictional or school-learning example. A private personal story is never required.
Work with a partner or table when talk improves the thinking; use the quiet observation route when you need it.
student.product: One Friday Learning Story with a specific example, a useful learning condition, one realistic goal, a first step, and a check date.
student.finish: You can point to a specific example, explain what it shows about your learning or contribution, and name one next step that is small enough to try.

student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Ask for today's image or question and one partner explanation. Choose one example you can genuinely explain.
student.spacesNote: One Friday Learning Story brings the week together. Monday–Thursday practice does not need separate posts.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: The first formed-class week
family.summary: Students are introduced through several kinds of classroom evidence: oral story and listening, number reasoning, learning conditions, exact place observations, collaboration, and reflection. No student is required to share a private or painful story.
family.whyThisMatters: One task cannot show the whole learner. The week gives the teacher multiple low-stakes ways to notice strengths, strategies, participation, supports, and questions before students choose one example for a Friday Learning Story.
family.whatStudentsDo: Monday begins with ordinary-object storytelling. Tuesday uses a visual number investigation. Wednesday names changeable learning conditions and supports. Thursday gathers place observations. Friday students synthesize one meaningful example and a realistic first goal.

quickReference.atSchool: Students tell, estimate, discuss, observe, create, and revise across five connected days.
quickReference.home: Nothing to finish or prepare at home. A short conversation about one specific example is welcome.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher observes strategies, listening, contribution, and revision. Friday's Learning Story is an early portfolio snapshot, not a final judgment.
quickReference.spaces: One Friday Learning Story is posted; the week's practice remains in class.

family.product: One student-selected Friday Learning Story with evidence of a strength or contribution, useful learning conditions, and one realistic goal.
family.assessment: Early formative evidence only. The teacher looks for specific examples, explanation, listening, strategy, revision, and a feasible next step.
family.agreementNote: Students may use fictional, observation-only, written, spoken, visual, or recorded routes. Private family, medical, diagnostic, or painful information is not required.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Pairs and groups create several opportunities to hear student thinking. The final Learning Story is individual so each learner chooses the evidence and goal that genuinely fit.

shared.title: Who decides—and what does this place teach us?
shared.bigQuestion: How can maps, sources, local voices, and public decisions change what we understand about Surrey?
shared.summary: Students use the existing place, map, evidence, perspective, and government lessons as a live Surrey case. They distinguish observation from inference, learn from attributed local-Nation and district sources, sort who controls which decisions, and begin checking election claims after the official candidate list is available.

learningArc.label: Who decides?
learningArc.studentAction: Sort school, district, city, provincial, and federal decisions; explain the exact authority involved.
learningArc.outcome: Students distinguish influence, administration, voting, oversight, and final authority.

learningArc.label: Learn with place
learningArc.studentAction: Gather local observations and compare what different maps and attributed sources make visible or leave out.
learningArc.outcome: Place learning remains specific to source, Nation, speaker, purpose, and protocol.

learningArc.label: Check a campaign claim
learningArc.studentAction: Label fact, opinion, claim, or promise; trace one checkable part to an official or independent source.
learningArc.outcome: A campaign statement becomes evidence to investigate, not a position students are told to support.

learningArc.label: Make meaning
learningArc.studentAction: Build a concise place-and-decision display with exact source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one next question.
learningArc.outcome: The display makes local learning visible without turning a generic craft into reconciliation.

learningArc.label: Carry it forward
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one election, place, or power question worth following in the October Newsroom.
learningArc.outcome: Strong questions continue; no extra SpacesEDU post is required.

visual.alt: A source desk with a Surrey map, dated article, photograph, notes, and question cards ready for students to compare.
visual.caption: Start with the source: look, locate, credit, compare, and keep one uncertainty visible.

thinkingMoves.label: Locate
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which place, decision, level of government, and date are involved?

thinkingMoves.label: Credit
thinkingMoves.prompt: Who made or shared this source, and whose knowledge or interest does it represent?

thinkingMoves.label: Separate
thinkingMoves.prompt: What is observed, stated, inferred, promised, or still unknown?

thinkingMoves.label: Compare
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which second source, map, or perspective changes the first picture?

thinkingMoves.label: Question
thinkingMoves.prompt: Whose perspective is missing, and what would be a respectful next source?

teacher.timing: Surrey, place, and election inquiry · Sept. 21–30
teacher.duration: Six to seven flexible blocks across eight school days
teacher.grouping: Whole-class source launches; pairs for close reading and claim checks; groups of 3–4 for jurisdiction sorting and display design; individual reflection only when each student's own question matters.
teacher.launch: We are going to look closely at decisions and sources connected to the place outside our classroom. Our job is not to choose a candidate. It is to work out who can decide, what the evidence supports, whose perspective is present, and what still needs checking.
prepare: Open the existing Social Studies lessons Three Maps of Fleetwood, Power Is Already in the Room or Same Crisis, Different Systems, Perspective Without Guessing, and Trace the Claim.
Use the Surrey election bridge and official source doors. After Sept. 11, use the official candidate information rather than provisional lists.

Select one exact Surrey Schools Indigenous Learning, local-Nation, FNESC, or First Nations-led source. Record speaker or author, Nation or organization, place, title, date, and sharing guidance before teaching.
Prepare a no-Wi-Fi route: source title and credit on the board, one short permitted excerpt or teacher notes, a projected or printed map, and notebooks.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Sort exact school, trustee, city, provincial, and federal scenarios; require the decision and authority, not only the topic.
Compare what a street map, planning map, and First Peoples' map make visible; keep source, purpose, and limits attached.
Return to local observation, then learn directly from one attributed local or district-curated source without turning it into a generic Indigenous claim.
Use stated evidence to identify who is affected and whose perspective is still missing; do not ask students to invent community voices.
Compare one dated campaign statement with the original official data, policy, budget, or jurisdiction source. Report supported, contradicted, or uncertain.
Groups build a concise display with source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one question. Use the Newsroom to choose what deserves following in October.

Separates observation, fact, opinion, claim, promise, inference, and uncertainty.
Uses evidence without inventing a missing person's or community's perspective.
Can explain how people who are not old enough to vote may still participate responsibly.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Use source notes, sorting talk, teacher observation, claim checks, and the shared display as formative evidence. student.title: Surrey: place, power, and an election
student.why: The city, school district, province, and Canada make different decisions. Sources help you work out who has the power, what a claim really says, and what is still missing.
student.summary: Look at maps, images, short texts, public information, and campaign statements. Discuss and investigate without being told which candidate or opinion is better.
student.grouping: Whole class, pairs, and teams of 3–4
bring: Pencil or another way to record
A source clue and a reason
student.firstMove: Point to one school, park, road, transit stop, recreation place, or neighbourhood feature on a Surrey map. Which public body might be able to change it—and what can it not decide alone?
student.firstMoveNote: Name the exact decision, not only a job title. Keep one uncertainty visible until a dated source helps you resolve it.

quickReference.firstMove: Choose one Surrey place. Name the exact decision and who might have authority.
quickReference.handIn: Keep your source notes and group display in class. No separate SpacesEDU post is planned.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the source, date, class question, and one clue. Add your own careful claim or question.

steps: Locate: find the place, date, and decision.
Sort: match the decision to school, district, city, province, or Canada.
Credit: name who made or shared each source.
Check: label fact, opinion, claim, or promise and trace one checkable part.
Compare: add another map, source, or perspective.
Explain: state what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain.
choices: Investigate through a map, image, short text, audio, or a teacher-read excerpt from the same credited source.
Compare a claim or missing perspective without endorsing or opposing a candidate.
Contribute by pointing, sorting, speaking, writing, or drawing; your teacher can provide a shared-screen or paper route.
student.product: A concise group display with exact source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one question worth following.
student.finish: You can identify who has authority for a decision, use a dated source as evidence, name a missing perspective without inventing it, and keep one uncertainty visible.
student.handInOrSave: Keep the display and source trail in class. Your teacher will say if one later reflection belongs in an existing portfolio pathway.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Begin with one visible clue and the source credit. Ask: Who made this? When? What exact decision or claim is involved?
student.spacesNote: Discussion, notebooks, and the class display are enough. No new SpacesEDU post is planned.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: Learning from Surrey's live election and local sources
family.summary: Students use the October 17 Surrey municipal and school-board election as one current case inside existing learning about maps, government, power, evidence, perspective, and place. The learning is politically neutral and does not ask students or families to declare support for a candidate.
family.whyThisMatters: Local decisions affect schools, parks, recreation, roads, transit, housing, services, taxes, and public spaces. Students learn which institution can act, how campaign claims can be checked, and how people can participate even before they are old enough to vote.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students sort real decision scenarios, examine maps and attributed local sources, distinguish fact/opinion/claim/promise, check one campaign statement against an original source, and build a concise place-and-decision display.

quickReference.atSchool: Students compare sources, sort who decides what, check claims, discuss trade-offs, and create a small evidence display.
quickReference.home: No campaign research or political discussion is required at home. Families may discuss one local decision that matters to young people.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher assesses use of evidence, jurisdiction, perspective, questions, and revision—not a student's political opinion.
quickReference.spaces: Most work stays in discussion, notebooks, and a classroom display; no extra post is planned.

family.product: One group display with source credit, a careful claim, a missing perspective, and an open question.
family.assessment: Formative assessment focuses on evidence, authority, source care, reasoning, uncertainty, and respectful discussion. Candidate preference is never assessed.
family.agreementNote: The class will use official election, city, school-district, and credible Canadian sources. Candidate statements are treated as claims to examine, not endorsements.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Teams compare and explain sources. The teacher also listens for each student's ability to point to evidence, distinguish authority from influence, and revise a claim.

milestones.label: Surrey election nominations close; official candidate information becomes the class source
Local place, decision-making, source, and election investigations

family.homework: No special supplies, candidate research, or routine homework are expected.
supportAtHome: Ask which Surrey decision the class sorted and who actually has authority.
Ask what made one source more useful or limited than another.
Discuss how a young person can ask questions, verify information, write, speak, create, volunteer, or attend public events without voting.
conversationPrompts: Which Surrey decision affects young people most, and who has the authority to act?
What is the difference between a campaign promise and evidence that it can happen?
Whose perspective was missing from one source the class examined?
family.spacesNote: Most work remains in class. The teacher may later select one student-authored reflection only if it adds meaningful evidence to an existing portfolio pathway.

shared.title: Before the vote: claims, responsibilities, and choices
shared.bigQuestion: How can we compare election choices without confusing a persuasive promise with evidence that it can happen?
shared.summary: Students continue the existing Surrey election case through Trace the Claim, the Newsroom, and Civic Decision Brief. They compare directly sourced statements about the same issue, check what mayor, council, and trustees can actually decide, weigh trade-offs, and prepare for the existing Student Vote process without adding another unit or portfolio post.

learningArc.label: Match power
learningArc.studentAction: Match candidate statements to the office's real responsibilities and flag anything that needs council, the Board of Education, the province, funding, or time.
learningArc.outcome: Students distinguish leadership and influence from decisions one winner can make alone.

learningArc.label: Trace a claim
learningArc.studentAction: Use Trace the Claim and a dated source trail to label fact, opinion, claim, or promise and verify one checkable part.
learningArc.outcome: Students report supported, contradicted, or still uncertain instead of reacting to confidence or style.

learningArc.label: Compare fairly
learningArc.studentAction: Place directly sourced statements about one issue on a common comparison board: proposal, evidence, authority, trade-off, missing perspective, and question.
learningArc.outcome: Candidates are compared by the same inquiry criteria without a teacher ranking or endorsement.

learningArc.label: Hear and question
learningArc.studentAction: Use the existing Civic Decision Brief hearing to present evidence, ask neutral follow-up questions, and revise one conclusion.
learningArc.outcome: Public reasoning stays separate from anyone's private ballot choice.

learningArc.label: Student Vote
learningArc.studentAction: Learn the ballot routine, serve in election-worker roles, and vote privately through the existing Student Vote structure when the class is registered.
learningArc.outcome: Students practise an election process after learning the offices, evidence, and responsibilities.

visual.alt: Grade 6 students using common evidence cards in a classroom civic hearing while classmates listen and prepare questions.
visual.caption: Use the same evidence questions for every candidate: What is proposed? Who has authority? What supports it? What is the trade-off?

thinkingMoves.label: Verify
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which part can be traced to an original, dated source?

thinkingMoves.label: Challenge assumptions
thinkingMoves.prompt: Are we assuming one person can decide what requires a council, board, budget, approval, or time?

thinkingMoves.label: Shift perspective
thinkingMoves.prompt: Who is affected, who is speaking, and whose view is still missing?

thinkingMoves.label: Weigh trade-offs
thinkingMoves.prompt: Who may benefit, what may it cost, and what could be given up?

thinkingMoves.label: Reflect
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which evidence changed or complicated our thinking?

teacher.timing: Surrey election comparison and Student Vote preparation · Oct. 1–16
teacher.duration: Five flexible blocks plus the existing Student Vote routine
teacher.grouping: Whole-class projector launches; pairs for claim tracing; teams of 3–4 for the common comparison board and civic hearing; a private individual ballot only because personal choice is the purpose.
teacher.launch: A campaign promise tells us what someone wants voters to believe or support. What else must we know before deciding whether the promise is possible, supported, and within that office's power?
prepare: Open the official City of Surrey candidate list and role descriptions through the existing Surrey election source doors; use directly sourced candidate material, not search snippets or unsourced comparison pages.

Choose one age-appropriate issue and short statements that can be compared with the same criteria. Include the date, speaker, office sought, original link, and enough context to avoid changing the meaning.
Open Trace the Claim, the Newsroom Quick Look or Deep Dive route, and Civic Decision Brief rather than building a second election lesson.
If the class is participating, use CIVIX Student Vote materials, ballots, and procedures. Classroom OS supports the learning; it does not duplicate the registration, election kit, or results system.
Prepare a projector-first and paper-card route. No student account or individual device is required.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Sort mayor, councillor, and trustee statements by what the office can lead, vote on collectively, influence, or not decide. Keep the six Surrey trustee seats visible alongside mayor and council.
Model one source trail on the projector, then have pairs check one statement and report supported, contradicted, or uncertain.
Teams compare statements on one issue using identical headings: proposal, evidence, authority, trade-off, missing perspective, question.
Run the existing Civic Decision Brief. Require sourced reasons and neutral questions; do not ask students to role-play a candidate or reveal a preference.
Review ballot privacy and election-worker roles, follow CIVIX procedures, and keep individual votes secret. Use the discussion and post-vote reflection as formative evidence, not the chosen name.

lookFors: Matches a promise to the actual authority of mayor, council, or the Board of Education.
Uses an original, dated source and preserves enough context to represent the statement fairly.
Separates fact, opinion, claim, promise, evidence, and uncertainty.
Applies the same comparison questions across candidates and can name a trade-off or missing perspective.
Explains a public conclusion without pressuring anyone to disclose a private ballot choice.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Keep claim trails, comparison talk, hearing questions, and the post-vote process reflection as formative classroom evidence. Do not assess candidate preference, publish individual ballots, or add a separate SpacesEDU post; connect a later student-selected reflection only if it strengthens an existing inquiry or Learning Story.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Check the promise before the vote
student.why: Candidates use facts, opinions, claims, and promises to persuade voters. You can check the source, the office's real power, and the trade-offs before making up your own mind.
student.summary: Work with a partner and team to trace one claim, compare statements with the same questions, take part in a civic hearing, and prepare for a private Student Vote ballot.
student.grouping: Pairs and teams for investigation; whole class for the hearing; a private individual ballot
bring: One source detail you can point to
A question that does not assume the answer
Respect for other people's private choices
student.firstMove: Read one short campaign statement. Underline the exact promise. Circle what could be checked. Put a question mark beside anything the office may not control alone.
student.firstMoveNote: A strong promise can still require a council or board vote, money, another level of government, public input, or time.

quickReference.firstMove: Underline the promise, circle the checkable part, and question the office's authority.
quickReference.handIn: Keep the pair claim trail and team comparison board in class. Your ballot choice stays private.
quickReference.missed: Open one dated statement and its original source. Add the office, one checkable claim, and one honest uncertainty.

steps: Identify: Who said it, when, and which office are they seeking?
Label: Is it a fact, opinion, claim, or promise?
Trace: Open the original source for the strongest checkable part.
Match: Can this office decide it alone, act with others, influence it, or not control it?
Compare: Use the same headings for every candidate statement.
Question: Ask about evidence, cost, trade-offs, missing perspectives, or what happens next.
Decide privately: Use the Student Vote ballot only after you understand the offices and evidence.
choices: Use a teacher-read excerpt, projected source, short text, audio, or paper source card with the same credit and context.
Contribute by pointing, sorting, speaking, writing, drawing a decision path, or asking a question.
Change your mind, remain uncertain, or keep your ballot choice private; your political preference is not assessed.
student.product: One pair claim trail, one team comparison board, and a short reflection on the evidence or process—not on which name you chose.
student.finish: You can check a campaign statement, explain what the office can and cannot do alone, compare choices fairly, and protect ballot privacy.
student.handInOrSave: Keep investigation notes and the comparison board in class. Follow the class Student Vote routine; never put your ballot choice in SpacesEDU.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Start with one statement and four questions: Who said it? What is promised? What evidence checks it? Who has the power to act?
student.spacesNote: No extra SpacesEDU post is planned. Your ballot choice remains private.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: Checking claims before Surrey's October 17 election
family.summary: Students compare candidate statements for Surrey mayor, council, and school trustee through existing civics and media-literacy lessons. The class uses neutral questions and directly sourced material; it does not recommend a candidate or ask families to share how they vote.
family.whyThisMatters: A promise may sound clear while still requiring a council or Board of Education vote, a budget, provincial action, public input, or time. Students learn to check both the evidence and the limits of an elected role.
family.whatStudentsDo: Pairs trace one campaign claim to its source, teams use the same comparison headings for candidates, and the class holds an evidence-based civic hearing. If registered, the class then follows CIVIX Student Vote procedures for a private mock ballot.

quickReference.atSchool: Students check claims, compare responsibilities and trade-offs, ask neutral questions, and practise a private Student Vote process.
quickReference.home: No candidate research, political disclosure, or election homework is required.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher assesses source use, jurisdiction, reasoning, questions, and revision—not political preference.
quickReference.spaces: Investigation and ballot work stay in class; no extra post is planned.

family.product: A pair source trail, a team comparison board, and a process reflection. Individual ballot choices are not collected as learning evidence.
family.assessment: Formative assessment focuses on careful source use, fair comparison, authority, trade-offs, uncertainty, and respectful participation—not political preference.
family.agreementNote: The Student Vote is a non-partisan classroom learning process. A student's choice is private and is not a prediction of, or instruction about, family voting.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Pairs and teams make reasoning visible. Any individual reflection concerns evidence and process; the name selected on a ballot remains private.

milestones.label: Candidate responsibilities, source checking, and fair comparison
Civic hearing and neutral follow-up questions
Student Vote classroom process, if the class is registered
Surrey municipal and school-board election day

family.homework: No routine homework or family political discussion is expected.
supportAtHome: Ask what part of a campaign statement was checkable and which source helped.
Ask whether the promise could be completed by one winner or required other people, money, approvals, or time.
Reassure your child that different views can be discussed respectfully and ballot choices remain private.
conversationPrompts: What is one question that should be asked about every campaign promise?
What can a school trustee decide only with the rest of the Board?
Which piece of evidence changed or complicated your thinking?
family.spacesNote: No additional portfolio post is planned, and individual Student Vote choices are never posted.

shared.eyebrow: OCTOBER · RESULTS AND WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
shared.title: Election day to next steps: what happens now?
shared.bigQuestion: What do election results tell us—and what still has to happen before a promise becomes a public decision?
shared.summary: Students use the Newsroom to read official Surrey results and CIVIX Student Vote results when each is released. They compare patterns carefully, follow one promise through the people, votes, budgets, approvals, and time it may require, and identify ways people can continue to influence public decisions after election day.

learningArc.label: Election day
learningArc.studentAction: Notice which Surrey offices are being elected and wait for official, dated results rather than reposting early claims or guesses.
learningArc.outcome: Students understand that result status and source matter.

learningArc.label: Read the results
learningArc.studentAction: Open the official Surrey results and record office, names, totals or shares, result status, source, and update time.
learningArc.outcome: The class builds an accurate result record for mayor, council, and school trustees.

learningArc.label: Compare carefully
learningArc.studentAction: Compare official and Student Vote results when both are available; describe a pattern without guessing why it happened.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate numerical patterns from unsupported explanations about voters.

learningArc.label: Follow a promise
learningArc.studentAction: Trace one promise through the council or board decision, staff work, budget, other approvals, public input, and time it may require.
learningArc.outcome: Winning an election is distinguished from having unlimited or immediate power.

learningArc.label: Keep participating
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one respectful next action a young person could take: follow a meeting, ask a question, write, verify, speak, create, volunteer, or revisit the evidence.
learningArc.outcome: Democratic participation continues between elections.

visual.alt: A newsroom source desk with a map, dated text, results chart, pencil, and magnifying glass ready for students to compare.
visual.caption: Record the source and result status first. Then describe the pattern, test explanations, and follow one promise into the real decision process.

thinkingMoves.label: Verify
thinkingMoves.prompt: Is this an official result, when was it updated, and is the count final?

thinkingMoves.label: Challenge assumptions
thinkingMoves.prompt: Does the result show why people voted, or are we guessing?

thinkingMoves.label: Investigate
thinkingMoves.prompt: Which decision path would this promise have to follow next?

thinkingMoves.label: Shift perspective
thinkingMoves.prompt: Whose priorities are visible in our sources, and whose are still missing?

thinkingMoves.label: Reflect
thinkingMoves.prompt: What can people still do after the ballots are counted?

teacher.timing: Surrey election results and reflection · Oct. 17–23
teacher.duration: One 10–15 minute Newsroom check plus two or three 25–45 minute blocks
teacher.grouping: Whole-class projector source checks; pairs for results reading; teams of 3–4 for promise pathways; individual reflection only when each student chooses a personal next action.
teacher.launch: An election chooses people for public roles. Does winning mean they can now do everything they promised? What evidence would show the difference between being elected and making a decision happen?
prepare: Open the official City of Surrey results only when released; display the source, update time, and result status. If results remain preliminary or incomplete, say so and return later.
Open CIVIX Student Vote results only when released after polls close. Keep the school or class ballot process private and follow CIVIX reporting directions.
Choose one promise already examined before the election. Reuse its source trail and the official mayor/council/trustee role descriptions.
Use the Newsroom Quick Look for the first result check and Deep Dive only if the comparison and decision pathway earn more time.
Prepare a paper or board path labelled WIN → COLLECTIVE DECISION → STAFF / DISTRICT WORK → MONEY / APPROVALS → PUBLIC INPUT → TIME → REVIEW.

runOfShow.teacherAction: Project the official source. Record what is known, the result status and update time, and one question. Do not fill gaps from social posts or memory.
Pairs describe one official/Student Vote similarity or difference when both are available. Separate what the numbers show from hypotheses about why.
Teams move one pre-election promise through the real pathway. Require the collective body, budget or approval, staff role, time, and review point that apply.
Students name a respectful way to keep following or influencing a public decision. Close with one question for a future Newsroom check rather than a new assignment.

lookFors: Records the official source, update time, and whether a result is preliminary or final.
Describes a numerical pattern without claiming it proves voters' motives.
Explains that mayor and councillors act through council and trustees through the Board of Education, with other people, rules, money, approvals, and time shaping outcomes.
Returns to a pre-election promise and identifies a realistic next decision or accountability point.
Names a specific, respectful way young people can continue participating.
teacher.evidenceHandoff: Use the result check, pair comparison, promise pathway, and discussion as formative evidence about source reading, quantitative reasoning, public institutions, and reflection. No new SpacesEDU post is required; the private ballot remains outside assessment and reporting.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Results are the beginning, not the end
student.why: Election results tell us who was chosen. They do not prove why everyone voted, and they do not give one winner unlimited power.
student.summary: Read official Surrey results, compare them with Student Vote results when available, follow one promise through the real decision path, and choose a way young people can keep participating.
student.grouping: Whole class, pairs, and teams; one short personal next-step reflection
bring: The source name and update time
One pattern the numbers actually show
One question about what happens next
student.firstMove: Find the result source, its update time, and its status. Write one sentence that begins, ‘This result shows…’ and one that begins, ‘This result does not show…’
student.firstMoveNote: Wait for official results. A total or percentage shows a pattern; it does not automatically explain people's reasons.

quickReference.firstMove: Record source, update time, and status. Say what the result shows and does not show.
quickReference.handIn: Keep the result note and promise pathway in class. No extra SpacesEDU post is planned.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the official result source and one promise. Add one accurate pattern and one next step the promise would require.

steps: Verify: use the official Surrey result and record when it was updated.
Describe: state one result pattern without guessing why people voted.
Compare: add Student Vote results when released and name one similarity or difference.
Trace: follow one promise through the people, collective vote, money, approvals, public input, and time it needs.
Question: identify what should be checked at a future council or Board meeting.
Continue: choose one respectful way a young person can follow or influence the issue.
choices: Read a projected chart, paper result table, teacher-read numbers, audio description, or the original result page.
Show a comparison by speaking, writing, pointing, arranging cards, or drawing the promise pathway.
Keep your ballot choice private and discuss results without guessing how classmates or families voted.
student.product: One accurate result note, one team promise pathway, and one question or next action worth carrying into a future Newsroom check.
student.finish: You can say what the results show and do not show, explain why winners still share power, and name a way participation continues.
student.handInOrSave: Keep the result note and pathway in class. Save the follow-up question for a future Newsroom check; do not post ballot choices.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Use one official result and one promise. Ask: What happened? What does the number not explain? Who must act next?
student.spacesNote: No extra SpacesEDU post is planned. Results discussion and ballot choices stay out of the portfolio.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: After Surrey votes: results, limits, and next steps
family.summary: Students read official Surrey election results and CIVIX Student Vote results when they become available. They practise describing numerical patterns carefully, then investigate what an elected mayor, councillor, or trustee must do with other people before a promise becomes a decision.
family.whyThisMatters: Winning an election grants a public role, not unlimited power. Council and the Board of Education make collective decisions, and many proposals also require staff work, budgets, approvals, public input, and time.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students verify the result source and status, compare official and Student Vote patterns without guessing at voters' motives, follow one earlier promise through a decision pathway, and identify ways participation continues after election day.

quickReference.atSchool: Students read results, compare patterns, trace one promise into the real public process, and ask what should be followed next.
quickReference.home: No election homework or disclosure of family voting is expected.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher assesses source reading, numerical interpretation, understanding of shared power, and thoughtful questions—not election preference.
quickReference.spaces: This is formative classroom learning; no extra portfolio post is planned.

family.product: A result note, a team promise pathway, and one question or participation step for a later Newsroom check.
family.assessment: Formative assessment looks for accurate source details, careful interpretation, understanding of collective authority, and a realistic next question or action.
family.agreementNote: Class discussion does not ask students to reveal their Student Vote choice or families to reveal a real ballot. Similarities and differences in results are examined without judging voters.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Pairs and teams make source and decision reasoning visible. A short individual next step may show personal agency without recording a political preference.

Ask which people, votes, budgets, approvals, or time one promise would need next.
Discuss one respectful way a young person can ask questions or follow a community decision between elections.
conversationPrompts: What surprised you in the results, and what evidence would help explain it?
Why can a winner not simply do everything promised?
What public decision would you like the class to check again later?
